opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I think about a lot, and I don't think there's a single clean answer. It depends on what you're optimizing for.

On the benefits side, byte-level or character-level models get rid of a lot of the brittleness that comes with subword tokenization. A tokenizer like BPE is trained once, separately from the model, on some fixed corpus, and then it's frozen. That causes all sorts of downstream problems. It's sensitive to small perturbations: a typo, odd capitalization, or an extra space can produce a completely different segmentation, and the model can behave surprisingly differently. The model also doesn't really "see" the characters inside a token, which is part of why models struggle with spelling, counting letters, or character-level manipulation. And there are real fairness issues across languages. Tokenizers tend to be trained on data that's heavily skewed toward English and other high-resource languages, so text in many other languages, especially non-Latin scripts, gets split into many more tokens. That means higher cost per query, less effective context length, and often worse performance for those speakers. Operating on bytes gives you a universal, language-agnostic interface. Every language and every script is represented the same way, and there's no out-of-vocabulary problem.

The big drawback is efficiency. Byte sequences are much longer, often four or five times longer for English and even more relative to some other scripts. With standard transformers, attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length, so naively training on bytes is expensive for both training and inference. You also lose the nice property that each step of the model processes a chunk of meaning roughly the size of a word. Each position carries less information, so the model has to spend capacity just composing characters into meaningful units.

So a lot of the interesting work, including what I've been thinking about, is trying to get the best of both worlds: keep the robustness and universality of operating on bytes, but have the model learn to compress or merge those bytes internally, so the expensive parts of the network run on a much shorter sequence. Instead of a fixed, heuristic tokenizer bolted on before training, the model learns its own segmentation end to end, ideally adapting to the input. That's the direction I find most promising. Tokenization isn't going away overnight, since subword models are very well optimized and work well in practice, but I think we're getting closer to models where tokenization is learned rather than hand-engineered.

r001.rationale: The response says byte- or character-level modeling avoids subword brittleness and sensitivity to typos, capitalization, and spacing changes.

r002.rationale: It says the model does not really “see” the characters inside a subword token, connecting this to difficulty with spelling, letter counting, and character manipulation.

r003.rationale: It identifies longer byte sequences as a drawback, noting they are often four or five times longer for English and even longer for some scripts.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really the question that motivated a lot of my recent work. I think the first thing to say is that subword tokenization, something like BPE, is kind of a necessary evil in modern language models. It works really well in practice, but it introduces a lot of weirdness. You get these fixed segmentations that are decided before training ever happens, and those segmentations are often linguistically arbitrary. You'll see a word split in a way that doesn't line up with morphemes at all. And then there are the downstream issues people have documented, things like models struggling with spelling or character-level manipulation, sensitivity to typos, the fact that tokenizers trained on mostly English data are much less efficient for other languages, so the same content costs more tokens and the model effectively sees a compressed, less-favorable view of those languages.

So the appeal of going to characters or bytes is that you get rid of all of that. You have a universal, tiny vocabulary. Every language and every script is treated the same way at the input level. You don't have out-of-vocabulary problems, you're robust to noise, and you remove this whole preprocessing stage that's a source of bias and brittleness. From a modeling-purity standpoint it's very attractive.

The drawback, and it's a big one, is sequence length. A byte-level sequence is something like four to five times longer than the subword sequence for the same English text, and with a standard Transformer, attention is quadratic, so that's expensive both in training and at inference time. And it's not just compute. The model now has to spend capacity learning things the tokenizer used to give it for free, like which bytes group together into word-like units. Early work on byte-level models showed you could get competitive quality, but you were paying a lot for it.

The way I think about it is that the right question isn't really "characters versus subwords." It's "where should the grouping happen, and should it be learned?" What's exciting about the more recent direction, and this is where my work on MrT5 sits, is making the byte-level model learn to compress its own input. You operate on raw bytes at the input, but after a few layers the model learns to delete or merge positions that aren't carrying much information, so the deeper, more expensive layers see a much shorter sequence. You get a lot of the efficiency of subword models back, but the segmentation is learned, it's contextual, and it adapts per language rather than being baked in from an English-centric vocabulary. In our experiments the compression you get is actually more uniform across languages than what BPE gives you, which I think is a really nice property.

So my honest weighing is that today, subword tokenization is still the pragmatic default if you just want the best model per dollar. But I think that's an artifact of the architectures we have, not a fundamental truth. If we can make byte-level models efficient enough, and I think we're getting there with dynamic compression approaches, then the benefits in robustness, fairness across languages, and just conceptual cleanliness are pretty compelling, and I'd expect the field to keep moving in that direction.

r001.rationale: It says subword models struggle with spelling and character-level manipulation and are sensitive to typos, then describes byte-level models as robust to noise and removing those issues.

r002.rationale: It contrasts fixed subword segmentations with modeling raw bytes, which lets the model process the underlying characters and learn its own groupings.

r003.rationale: It identifies sequence length as a major drawback and says byte-level sequences are about four to five times longer for the same English text.

astra-6.text:
I think the main tradeoff is between flexibility and computational efficiency. With character-level or byte-level models, you don’t have to commit to a vocabulary of subword units ahead of time. A byte-level model can represent any text, and it exposes spelling and other information that subword tokenization can obscure. That can be useful for handling unusual words, typos, or languages that a particular tokenizer represents poorly.

The drawback is that your sequences get much longer. With a fixed context window, you can fit less text, and the model has to spend computation learning how those smaller units compose into words and larger structures. Bytes also don’t line up neatly with characters across writing systems, so byte-level modeling doesn’t automatically make everything equally efficient across languages.

Subword tokenization provides a useful shortcut: common sequences become single units, which makes processing more efficient. But those boundaries aren’t necessarily linguistically meaningful, and the tokenizer introduces its own biases. So I’d weigh the flexibility of the representation against the cost of learning and processing it—and consider whether a hierarchical approach could capture some of the benefits of both.

r001.rationale: The response says character or byte models can help with typos, but does not clearly state that they mitigate sensitivity to character-level manipulations compared with subword tokenization.

r002.rationale: It says byte-level modeling exposes spelling information that subword tokenization can obscure, communicating greater access to the characters within subword tokens.

r003.rationale: It explicitly identifies much longer sequences as a drawback of character-level or byte-level modeling.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main tradeoff is between flexibility and computational efficiency. With characters or bytes, you don’t have to commit to a fixed vocabulary of subword units. You can represent unusual words, different languages, spelling variations—all without deciding ahead of time which strings deserve their own tokens. Bytes are especially appealing because you can represent any text encoded as bytes with a very small vocabulary.

But you’re also making the sequences much longer. A word that might be one or two subword tokens becomes many character or byte tokens, so the model has to do more work to process the same amount of text. And it has to learn how those smaller units compose into useful linguistic patterns.

Subword tokenization gives you a practical shortcut: common sequences are already grouped together, which makes training and inference more efficient. But the segmentation can be quite uneven across languages, and it can make things like spelling or reasoning about individual letters awkward because the model doesn’t directly see those letters as separate units.

So I wouldn’t say one is universally better. The interesting question is whether we can get the flexibility of byte-level input while learning to build larger units efficiently, instead of fixing those units before training.

r001.rationale: The response mentions spelling variations, but does not say character or byte modeling reduces sensitivity to character-level manipulations.

r002.rationale: It says subword models do not directly see individual letters, making spelling or letter-level reasoning awkward.

r003.rationale: It explicitly identifies longer character or byte sequences as requiring more work than subword tokens.
